info.title: Sizing and reserving crash kernel memory

abstract.para: Before &kdump; can capture a crash dump, a dedicated area of memory must be reserved for the capture kernel. Use kdumptool calibrate to determine a suitable size, or set it manually if the automatic value is not sufficient. kdumptool is part of the kdump package. See if it is not installed yet.

section.title: Using the automatically calculated size
section.para: By default, KDUMP_CRASHKERNEL in /etc/sysconfig/kdump is set to auto. With this setting, kdumptool commandline derives the crash kernel memory size from kdumptool calibrate automatically. You do not need to calculate or set anything manually to get started. Run the calibration tool directly to see the values it would use:

example.title: Determining the recommended crash kernel memory size
example.screen: Total: 4095 Low: 72 High: 384 MinLow: 72 MaxLow: 666 MinHigh: 0 MaxHigh: 2048 NonCMA: 300 CMA: 640

section.para: All values are given in megabytes. On &x86-64;, Low is the recommended reservation in the DMA32 zone (memory up to the 4 GiB mark), and High is the recommended reservation from the remaining available memory. On the other architectures, the whole reservation is reported as Low, and High is 0. MinLow/ MaxLow and MinHigh/MaxHigh give the valid range around those recommendations. NonCMA and CMA are the suggested sizes for the two parts of the reservation when KDUMP_USE_CMA is enabled. See .

note.title: Calibrated values depend on the system
note.para: The exact numbers returned by kdumptool calibrate depend on the amount of RAM and the hardware configuration of the machine it runs on. Always run it on the target system itself rather than reusing values from another machine.

section.title: Crash kernel memory formats
section.para: When you set KDUMP_CRASHKERNEL manually, the value is either auto or one or more crashkernel= options in one of these formats:

listitem.para: crashkernel=SIZE[@OFFSET] reserves a fixed amount of memory, for example crashkernel=256M. The optional offset is the physical address where the reserved area starts. A suitable size is the sum of the Low and High values from kdumptool calibrate. On architectures other than &x86-64;, auto produces this form.

crashkernel=SIZE_LOWM,low crashkernel=SIZE_HIGHM,high reserves one area below the 4 GiB mark and one from the remaining memory, for example crashkernel=72M,low crashkernel=384M,high. On &x86-64;, auto produces this form when kdumptool calibrate reports a Low value above 0. Otherwise, it sets only the ,high value.

crashkernel=RANGE1:SIZE1[,RANGE2:SIZE2,...][@OFFSET] reserves a size that depends on the amount of installed RAM. Each range has the form START-[END], where the start is inclusive and the end is exclusive. For example, crashkernel=512M-2G:64M,2G-:128M reserves:
Nothing on systems with less than 512 MiB of RAM.
64 MiB on systems with 512 MiB up to but not including 2 GiB.
128 MiB on systems with 2 GiB or more.

section.para: Override the automatically calculated reservation manually if it is not sufficient, for example, if &kdump; still runs out of memory while capturing a dump. section.remark: ssarkar: the LUN-based adjustment is carried forward from the SLE 15 tuning guide. kdumptool calibrate does not count LUNs and man 7 kdump does not mention them, so nothing in the current tools backs the formula. Asked the kdump SME on PR #802 whether it is still valid.

section.title: Reducing the required memory by excluding unused devices on &zseries;
section.para: Depending on the number of available devices, the calculated crash kernel memory may not be sufficient. Instead of increasing the value, you can limit the number of devices that the capture kernel sees. The kernel does not detect devices on the cio_ignore blocklist and does not allocate memory for them, so the capture kernel needs less memory.

step.para: Create a blocklist that contains all devices that are currently offline, and print it as a kernel parameter:

The command prints a cio_ignore= parameter that blocks all devices except the ones that are currently online. The new blocklist takes effect immediately and replaces any existing blocklist. Unused devices are not purged, so they still appear in the channel subsystem. Channel devices that you add afterward, with CP ATTACH under z/VM or by a dynamic I/O configuration change in an LPAR, are treated as blocked. To keep the original setting, run cio_ignore -l first and revert to that state after running cio_ignore -u -k.
Add the printed parameter to KDUMP_COMMANDLINE_APPEND in /etc/sysconfig/kdump:

section.remark: ssarkar: carried forward from the SLE 15 tuning guide. The cio_ignore options and their effect match cio_ignore(8) from s390-tools, which lists cio_ignore -u -k as an example, and kdump's load.sh passes KDUMP_COMMANDLINE_APPEND to the capture kernel. Not run on IBM Z, and the kdump SME did not verify it (PR #802). Needs a reviewer for IBM Z.

section.title: Applying a changed reservation
section.para: After changing KDUMP_CRASHKERNEL, a full system reboot is required, since the crash kernel memory reservation is applied at boot time. See for how the new value is picked up.
